# Topic at a Glance

> **One-sentence summary:** t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) maps high-dimensional observations to two or three dimensions by making nearby pairs remain probable neighbors, creating an exploratory display of local structure rather than a metrically faithful global map.

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| **Biological question** | Which cells or samples form locally similar neighborhoods, and are there possible rare states or transitions to investigate? |
| **Computational problem** | Produce a low-dimensional layout whose neighborhood probabilities resemble those in the input space |
| **Method type** | Nonlinear, stochastic dimensionality reduction for visualization |
| **Input** | A filtered, normalized feature matrix or, commonly, a PCA representation; perplexity and optimization settings |
| **Output** | Two- or three-dimensional coordinates for each observation |
| **Bioinformatics uses** | Exploratory views of single-cell, cytometry, proteomic, and population-genetic data |
| **Prerequisites** | [PCA](principal-component-analysis-for-omics-data.qmd), distances, conditional probabilities, and [k-nearest-neighbor graphs](k-nearest-neighbor-graphs.qmd) |

# What t-SNE preserves—and what it does not

t-SNE turns high-dimensional pairwise closeness into probabilities. In the input space, each observation $i$ assigns high conditional probability to close observations $j$. In the map, nearby points are also assigned high probability. The layout is optimized so these distributions agree as well as possible.

```text
quality-controlled high-dimensional data
    -> usually reduce noise with PCA
    -> convert local distances to neighbor probabilities
    -> initialize 2D/3D points
    -> optimize probability matching
    -> inspect local neighborhoods with metadata and markers
```

The map is especially useful for asking, “which observations are local neighbors?” It is not reliable for reading the distance between well-separated islands, their area, their density, or the apparent width of a trajectory. Different runs can rotate, reflect, or rearrange global positions while preserving useful local neighborhoods.

# The probability model

For high-dimensional points $x_i$, t-SNE uses a Gaussian conditional neighborhood distribution

$$
p_{j\mid i}=\frac{\exp\left(-\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2/(2\sigma_i^2)\right)}{\sum_{k\ne i}\exp\left(-\lVert x_i-x_k\rVert^2/(2\sigma_i^2)\right)}.
$$

The bandwidth $\sigma_i$ is chosen separately for each observation so that the distribution has a user-selected **perplexity**, an effective neighborhood size. Symmetrized pair probabilities $p_{ij}$ define the similarities t-SNE tries to retain.

For low-dimensional coordinates $y_i$, t-SNE uses a heavy-tailed Student $t$ distribution,

$$
q_{ij}=\frac{(1+\lVert y_i-y_j\rVert^2)^{-1}}{\sum_{k\ne l}(1+\lVert y_k-y_l\rVert^2)^{-1}},
$$

and minimizes the Kullback--Leibler divergence

$$
\mathrm{KL}(P\parallel Q)=\sum_{i\ne j}p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}.
$$

The heavy tail supplies stronger long-range repulsion than a Gaussian map, helping prevent the “crowding problem” in which many moderately distant neighbors must fit into a small visual area. Because the objective weights preserving high $p_{ij}$ strongly, local errors matter more than global geometry.

# A small mental model

Imagine three groups of cells: a compact group A, a compact group B, and a gradual set of intermediate cells. Each cell distributes most of its input-space probability among its close neighbors. During optimization, the map pulls high-probability pairs together and pushes all points apart.

If A and B have few cross-neighbor pairs, they may appear as distinct islands. The gap between those islands is not an estimate of biological divergence: t-SNE can enlarge or shrink it with optimization settings. If intermediate cells lack enough sampled neighbors, the map may break a continuous biological process into islands. Conversely, an apparent bridge may arise from doublets or technical mixing. Inspect original-space neighbors, known markers, and experimental provenance before making either claim.

# Parameters and reproducible use

| Setting | Role | Practical interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Perplexity | Effective neighborhood size used to set $\sigma_i$ | Test values appropriate to sample size; small values emphasize very local structure |
| Learning rate | Gradient-descent step scale | Too low can converge slowly; too high can destabilize the layout |
| Early exaggeration | Temporarily strengthens attractive forces early in optimization | Often improves separation, but changes visual appearance |
| Iterations / convergence | Optimization budget | Check objective behavior and repeat from several seeds |
| Initialization | Starting coordinates, often PCA-based | Affects reproducibility and sometimes global arrangement |
| Input dimensions | Representation supplied to t-SNE | PCA on appropriate features commonly denoises and accelerates the analysis |

Use the same preprocessing and random seed when a layout must be reproduced. Re-run a small set of justified parameter values and compare local neighbor preservation, not whether a desired picture looks most separated. Barnes--Hut and interpolation-based approximations make large datasets feasible, but software choices can change the exact optimization.

# Reading an omics t-SNE responsibly

1. Start with assay-appropriate QC, normalization, transformation, and feature selection. For single-cell RNA-seq, run t-SNE on a documented PCA representation rather than raw count vectors.
2. Overlay pre-existing metadata and independent features, such as batch, donor, cell-cycle score, or canonical markers. These distinguish hypotheses from visual artifacts.
3. Cross-check a proposed local group in the input-space [kNN graph](k-nearest-neighbor-graphs.qmd) and quantify it with an appropriate downstream analysis.
4. Use a separate statistical design for differential expression, abundance changes, or clinical association. A two-dimensional layout is not a significance test.

| Tempting interpretation | Why it fails | Better question |
|---|---|---|
| “This larger island contains more cells.” | Layout area and density are optimization artifacts | How many cells are in the group? Count them directly. |
| “A wider gap means more different cell types.” | Global distances are weakly constrained | Are the groups separated in the original representation and supported by markers? |
| “Each island is a cell type.” | t-SNE can separate continuous or batch-driven variation | Do replicated samples, markers, and graph neighborhoods support the label? |
| “No overlap means no transition.” | Sampling and perplexity can create gaps | Examine trajectories and local neighborhoods in original space. |

# Limitations and alternatives

t-SNE is mainly a visualization method. It does not provide an inverse transform for placing future samples in the original formulation, a unique global coordinate system, or an automatic cluster count. It can be computationally expensive and its stochastic objective permits several visually different yet similarly good solutions.

UMAP is often selected for fast large-data embeddings and can support transform-like workflows in common implementations, but it has its own graph and parameter dependencies. Diffusion maps model connectivity through a diffusion operator and can be useful for continuous processes. [PCA](principal-component-analysis-for-omics-data.qmd) remains the more directly interpretable linear baseline. For grouping observations, use a validated clustering method on a documented representation or graph, rather than drawing cluster boundaries from a t-SNE image.

# Take-home Messages

1. t-SNE preserves local neighborhood probabilities for exploratory visualization, not global distances, cluster areas, or density.
2. Perplexity, input preprocessing, initialization, and optimization settings materially affect the display and must be reported.
3. A visually separated island is a hypothesis to validate with original-space neighbors, metadata, marker evidence, and replication.
4. Use t-SNE alongside—not instead of—QC, graph analysis, clustering validation, and statistical inference.
